discovery: Theory of defect-mediated two-dimensional melting and the prediction of the hexatic phase

nominees.name: A. Peter Young
nominees.affiliation: University of California, Santa Cruz, USA

subfield: Condensed matter physics (statistical mechanics of ordered phases and topological defects)
motivation: Halperin, Nelson and Young (1978-79) extended the Kosterlitz-Thouless picture to two-dimensional crystals. They showed that melting proceeds in two continuous steps: dislocation unbinding destroys translational order but leaves quasi-long-range bond-orientational order, and disclination unbinding later destroys that order too. The intermediate hexatic phase they predicted is a new state of matter, defined by a broken symmetry nobody had considered before. Experiments later confirmed it in free-standing liquid-crystal films, colloidal monolayers, electrons on helium and magnetic vortex lattices, and bond-orientational order has since become a standard idea in the physics of liquids, glasses, membranes and active matter. The 2016 prize honoured topological phase transitions. The HNY theory is the natural companion to that prize, because it turned topological defects into a way to classify phases of matter.
